questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend writing a short project document instead of relying on a live demo alone?
options: Because demos are never allowed in ServiceNow interviews
So you're recalling a story you've already carefully told yourself once, instead of inventing one live under interview pressure
Because a written document is required for ServiceNow certification
Because interviewers refuse to look at a working build
questions.explain: A write-up fixes your reasoning once, in advance, so you're not reconstructing it on the spot during an interview.

questions.q: What is the first component a project write-up should establish, per this lesson?
options: A list of every table and script used in the build
The business problem — a real situation, stated before any mention of the solution
A percentage improvement metric
The exact ServiceNow release version used
questions.explain: Stating the real problem first gives an interviewer the context to evaluate whether the solution actually fit it.

questions.q: Which component does this lesson say most candidates skip, even though it matters most?
options: What was actually built
The architecture and design decisions, and the reasoning behind them
The project's title
The list of certifications the candidate holds
questions.explain: A decision without its reasoning attached is just a fact — easily second-guessed and impossible to defend, which is exactly why course 13's ADR habit applies here.

questions.q: What does "what you'd do differently with more time or scale" demonstrate, according to this lesson?
options: That the original project was a failure
Judgment about the real limits of a lab-scale build, which is exactly what Architect-track and senior Developer-track interviews test for
Nothing useful — this component can be safely skipped
That the candidate should have used a different ServiceNow module entirely
questions.explain: Naming a lab build's real limits honestly, and what would change at real scale, shows the kind of judgment senior-level interviews are actually probing for.

questions.q: How does this lesson say the four-part structure should apply to the capstone built in Chapters 4 through 6?
options: It doesn't apply — the upcoming capstone needs a completely different documentation approach
Only the "what was built" component applies; the other three are optional
The same four components apply, written as you go — including your own ADRs for the design decisions, the same habit from course 13
The write-up should be written only after the entire capstone and job search are both complete
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties the upcoming capstone back to this same structure, recommending ADRs be written while the reasoning is still fresh, not reconstructed afterward.
